text:
A test can tell you that an effect is there. It can't tell you how big it is. Take two groups of three hundred thousand, on a score that varies by about fifteen points. Group B's average is higher by about a seventh of a point. The p-value is under three in ten thousand... highly significant. But a seventh of a point, against a spread of fifteen, is less than one percent of a standard deviation. It's real... and it's far too small to matter. With enough data, almost any difference passes a test. So passing stops telling you whether to care. What you need is a measure of size.

Cohen's d is the gap between two averages, counted in standard deviations. It has no units. A d of one means the averages sit one full standard deviation apart. Cohen called zero point two small, zero point five medium, and zero point eight large. Even large leaves a lot of overlap. At zero point eight, the two curves still share more than two thirds of their area. The labels are only a start. What counts as big depends on what's at stake. And unlike a p-value, a size doesn't depend on how much data you have.

Here the true effect is fixed at zero point three. Now grow the sample, from twenty per group to fifty thousand. The p-value plunges, from zero point one five to a number so small it prints as zero. But d just settles... near zero point three. The effect size is a fact about the world. The p-value is a fact about the world AND your sample. When the outcome is yes or no, there are two ways to say the size.

Say a new checkout button lifts conversion from three percent to four point two. That's forty percent more... or one point two percentage points. The first sounds bigger. Report both, so a reader can judge. And give every effect size an interval. Here, a d of zero point three six, plausibly anywhere from zero point one to zero point six. How big, how precise, and whether it's there at all. Report all three. But even a well measured effect can mean something other than it seems.
